Germany had fewer hospital infections per 100 patients than the European average in 2011–12. But when infections were measured across the population, Germany had more. Researchers linked this difference to Germany’s high level of hospital use.

## Nearly half a million hospital infections in one year

Some patients pick up a new infection while receiving hospital care, separate from the illness that brought them to hospital in the first place. These are known as healthcare-associated infections. In 2011, Germany had an estimated 478,000 cases of five common types, with around 16,000 deaths attributed to them [@zacher2019]. Earlier research cited in the study suggested that around 20–30% of these infections could be prevented.

Comparing hospital safety between countries is not as simple as it might seem, because the result can change depending on what is being measured. This post looks at two questions:

1. Is Germany's hospital infection problem worse than the European average?
2. Is the most common infection also the most harmful?

## Where the numbers come from

The figures come from a study by Zacher and colleagues, published in *Eurosurveillance* [@zacher2019]. The study used hospital survey data collected in 2011–12 by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). In each hospital, researchers recorded which patients had an infection on the day of the survey.

The German sample included about 9,600 patients from 46 randomly selected hospitals. The European average was based on about 274,000 patients from 1,149 hospitals across the European Union and European Economic Area (EU/EEA).

The researchers used these survey results to estimate how many new infections occurred over a year. They also estimated the harm caused by these infections using disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), a measure of healthy years lost through early death or time lived in poor health. In other words, an infection that causes little lasting harm does not count the same as one that causes severe illness or death.

## Below the European average per patient, above it across the population

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Germany had fewer infections per hospital patient but more per 100,000 people than the European (EU/EEA) average, 2011–12."

# Values reported in Zacher et al. (2019), rounded for readers
germany_vs_eu <- tibble(
  `How it is counted` = c(
    "New infections per 100 hospital patients",
    "New infections per 100,000 people",
    "Healthy years lost per 100,000 people"
  ),
  Germany = c("2.4", "592", "308"),
  `European average` = c("2.8", "468", "290"),
  `What the comparison suggests` = c(
    "Lower in Germany",
    "Higher in Germany",
    "Difference uncertain"
  )
)

knitr::kable(germany_vs_eu, align = "lrrl")
```
*Note: The study reported substantial uncertainty around the comparison in healthy years lost.*

Whether Germany looked better or worse depended on how infections were counted (@tbl-compare). For every 100 hospital patients, Germany had 2.4 new infections, compared with the European average of 2.8. But when the same infections were counted across the whole population, the order flipped: Germany had 592 infections per 100,000 people, compared with the European average of 468.

How could both be true? The researchers linked this reversal to Germany's high level of hospital use. At the time, Germany had the highest number of acute-care hospital beds in Europe and the second-highest rate of hospital patients per 1,000 people among 34 OECD countries. They also suggested that good hygiene may partly explain Germany's lower rate per patient. At the same time, the large number of people passing through hospitals could help explain why infections were more common across the population.

So, was Germany's problem worse? Measured across the population, there were more infections. Whether this led to greater overall health loss was less clear. Germany lost an estimated 308 healthy years per 100,000 people, compared with the European average of 290, but the uncertainty around this comparison was wide.

## The most common infection was not the most harmful

Counting cases treats every infection the same. Looking at healthy years lost shows which infections caused the greatest health loss (@fig-shares).

```{r}
#| label: fig-shares
#| fig-cap: "Pneumonia and bloodstream infections (blue) made up a larger share of healthy years lost than of infections. Germany, 2011. Shares calculated from Zacher et al. (2019)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5

# Cases and healthy years lost (DALYs) for each infection type in Germany
hai_germany <- tibble(
  infection = c(
    "Pneumonia",
    "Urinary tract infection",
    "Bloodstream infection",
    "Surgical wound infection",
    "C. difficile gut infection"
  ),
  cases = c(106586, 214150, 26976, 93222, 36002),
  dalys = c(69508, 66701, 58350, 28842, 20890)
)

# Totals for all five types
total_cases <- 478222
total_dalys <- 248920

hai_shares <- hai_germany |>
  mutate(
    `Share of infections` = cases / total_cases * 100,
    `Share of healthy years lost` = dalys / total_dalys * 100,
    highlight = ifelse(infection == "Pneumonia" | infection == "Bloodstream infection",
                       "Yes", "No")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Share of infections`, `Share of healthy years lost`),
    names_to = "share_type",
    values_to = "percent"
  ) |>
  mutate(share_type = factor(share_type,
                             levels = c("Share of infections", "Share of healthy years lost")))

ggplot(
  hai_shares,
  aes(
    x = percent,
    y = fct_reorder(infection, dalys),
    fill = highlight
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent), "%")),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ share_type) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#006DAE", "No" = "grey70"),
                    guide = "none") +
  expand_limits(x = 55) +
  labs(
    x = "Percentage of the total for all five infection types",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
